title: Three times, "read"
hook: the angel presses him and says read, three times, and then the first five verses (96:1–5; Bukhari)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ramadan, the month the book arrived, and its hidden Night of Power, better than a thousand months. Your line was: the night it came.

Read. I am not a reader. That exchange happens once in the cave, then again, then a third time. In between, the hadith says, the angel takes hold of him and presses him until he can hardly bear it. It's a strange, rough beginning: not a vision of light, but a grip, a word repeated, and a man saying he can't. Today's word is about the repeating: three times.
screen: `READ. I AM NOT A READER.` → `PRESSED, AND RELEASED.` → `THREE TIMES.`

segments.voice: The account is in Sahih al-Bukhari, told by 'Aishah. The angel came to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ in the cave and said: read. He answered, in Arabic, ma ana bi-qari'. The wording reads most naturally as a denial: I am not one who reads, I can't. Some scholars, pointing to other narrations worded differently, also hear a question: what shall I read? Then the angel took hold of him and pressed him hard, released him, and said again: read. The same answer. A second pressing. Read. The same answer. A third pressing. And then the angel didn't ask. He recited. In Pickthall's words: "Read: In the name of thy Lord Who createth, Createth man from a clot." And a few lines on: "Teacheth man that which he knew not." The order matters. The command doesn't come with the ability attached. He says he can't, three times, and the words come anyway, recited to him. He carries them home, his heart trembling, the hadith says. Qur'an lessons still have something of that night's shape: a line heard, said back, heard again, until it stays. And in Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet says the one skilled in the Qur'an will be with the noble, honored scribes, and the one who recites it with difficulty, struggling over it, gets a double reward. The struggle counts.
screen: `MA ANA BI-QARI'.` · `PRESSED, THEN ASKED AGAIN.` · `THE WORDS COME ANYWAY.` · `A DOUBLE REWARD FOR STRUGGLING.` · then, large: `READ, AND READ AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Take one short passage that's hard for you, a verse, a poem, a paragraph, and read it three times, slowly: once without trying to understand it all, once listening for one word that catches, once letting it stay. If you pray, you can use the line from today: read, in the name of thy Lord.
Three times. The angel said read, and the Prophet said I am not a reader, three times, before the first verses of surah ninety-six were given to him. Today's word.
Your line: read, and read again. The one who struggles still gets a double reward. That's day seven hundred twenty-four.

howItsDone: Muslims memorize and learn the Qur'an by repetition, reciting a passage aloud to a teacher again and again until it is held by heart.

notes: The two readings of ma ana bi-qari' (negation vs. interrogative ma) are attributed to 'scholars'; confirm fair and that the hadith leaves it open (some narrations have 'ma aqra'?' or 'kayfa aqra'?').
Index hook says 'the first five verses'; the script quotes 96:1–2 and 96:5 and does not state a count. Year 1 day 86 quoted 96:1–5 in full.
Pickthall 96:1–2 and 96:5 copied from the year-1 script; confirm wording.
Sahih al-Bukhari 4937: confirm number (also Sahih Muslim 798).

Editor: 'Muslims learn the Qur'an the way that night began' (a blanket claim) softened to 'Qur'an lessons still have something of that night's shape'; varied the 'notice' cue and dropped the stock 'that's the line for today' close. Note Bukhari 3 itself recites 96:1–3; the run to 96:5 is in other narrations (e.g. Bukhari 4953); confirm.

Audit: 'both readings have defenders, and the hadith doesn't decide' overstated the case; with the ba', ma ana bi-qari' is grammatically a denial, and the question reading leans on other narrations (ma aqra'?). Teach, myth reveal and trapdoor corrected. 'And it ends' (96:5 is not the end of the surah, and Bukhari 3 stops at 96:3) changed to 'a few lines on'; 'given to him whole' (could imply the whole Qur'an) to 'recited to him'.
